title: CuTe DSL Calling Conventions for GPU Kernel Development
key_concepts: Execution contexts: Python, Host JIT, Device Kernel
critical_patterns: Python → @cute.jit: Entry point for calling JIT functions from Python
Multi-Kernel Pipeline: Sequential execution of multiple kernels
Conditional Kernel Selection: Choosing kernels based on input size
Iterative Kernel Calls: Looping within a single kernel launch
constraints: Static arguments must be known at compile time
Dynamic arguments are passed at runtime
Tensors are passed by reference, no copying
compressed_summary: CuTe DSL provides a structured approach to writing GPU kernels with specific calling conventions that dictate whether function calls occur at compile time or runtime. The DSL operates within three execution contexts: Python, Host JIT, and Device Kernel. Python can call @cute.jit functions directly but must use a .launch() method from a @cute.jit function to invoke @cute.kernel functions due to the need for specifying grid and block configurations. JIT functions can call other JIT functions and Python functions, with these calls being inlined at compile time, resulting in zero overhead. Kernels can call JIT functions, also inlined, but cannot call other kernels dynamically, as CuTe DSL does not support CUDA Dynamic Parallelism. Arguments passed to kernels can be static, known at compile time, or dynamic, determined at runtime, affecting optimization opportunities. Tensors are always passed by reference, ensuring no copying occurs. Common patterns include multi-kernel pipelines, conditional kernel selection based on input size, and iterative kernel calls. Performance considerations emphasize the trade-offs between inlined calls and separate kernel launches, with a focus on minimizing launch overhead. Debugging tools include call tracing and print statements for both compile-time and runtime diagnostics. The document concludes with a decision tree for selecting the appropriate calling pattern based on specific needs and links to further resources on JIT caching, control flow, and real-world examples.
